Percy learned something huge about his friend and about the monster. Why might he keep asking questions even though he is scared?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy keeps asking because he feels unsafe and confused. Read the sentence around the word, guess its meaning, and then add the word, a definition in your own words, and a quick sketch or example to your Unit Vocabulary graphic organizer."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Let's model with *lashed*. I read the sentence on p. 44 about the storm. The storm is not just hitting the car. *Lashed* sounds like a whip, so I think it means struck with force, over and over. Whips and lashes are harsh, which makes the weather feel angry."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Look at *swerved* on p. 46. What clues in the sentence and the sentences near it help you figure out what it means?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The clues are that something is suddenly in the way and the car moves fast. I think swerved means the car turned quickly to the side to avoid hitting something."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which word describes a sound, *bleat* or *bulging*? How do you know, and what does that sound tell us about Grover?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Bleat is the sound. It is the sound goats make, so it hints that Grover is part goat. It also sounds shaky and scared, so it shows his panic."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Do not spend more than a minute on each word. Say the word, have students point to it in the text, give a quick context clue, and move on. Students finish their organizers in pairs. Note that *numb*, *wedged*, and *slumped* have physical and emotional uses. Ask for both when time allows."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Say only the clues you want students to notice. Check that students are using the sentence in the book and not only guessing from the word's sound."}]},{"id":"lab-review-game","title":"Unit Vocabulary Review","minutes":4,"standards":["L.6.4","L.6.6"],"routine":"Quick Review Game","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"With a partner, look at your Unit Vocabulary graphic organizer. Take turns. One partner reads a definition or acts out a word from an earlier lesson or today's list. The other partner names the word and uses it in a sentence about the story. Switch roles after each word."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"You have been collecting words all unit. Let's see how many you can remember and use. Give a definition, a gesture, or a sentence with a blank, and your partner names the word."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which word from today could you use to describe the storm? Which could describe Grover?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Lashed could describe the storm because it hit the car hard. Irritated or bleat could describe Grover, because he is upset and his voice sounds like a scared goat."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in using new vocabulary orally and in writing with expanded noun phrases.","sayAsk":"Say: Let's use words to add details to nouns. Ask: Which word gives your partner the best picture of Grover's fear? Allow students to review words in their home language before saying them in English.","watchFor":"If students give only a one-word definition, then prompt: 'Use it in a sentence about the story.' If students use a word incorrectly, then have them find it on the page and read the sentence again. Success: students use at least two Chapter 4 words correctly in a sentence with an expanded noun phrase."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: remembering and using new words","tryTo":"","tryThis":"Give students a word bank with the ten words, a picture or gesture for each, and the frame 'In the story, ___ means ___ when ___.' Have them practice with only three words before moving on."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: precision of word choice","tryThis":"Ask students to pick two words with similar meanings (for example *irritated* and *furious*) and explain which one fits Grover or Percy better and why."}]}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Students cite dialogue and description from pp. 44–50 to analyze how the truth is slowly revealed, how word choice builds tension and drives action, and what Percy's questions and reactions suggest about values and fears.","activities":[{"id":"lia-close-read-dialogue","title":"Track the Slow Reveal","minutes":10,"standards":["RL.6.1","L.6.6"],"routine":"Close Read and Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 4","pages":"pp. 44–50"},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread pp. 44–50. Make a two-column chart. In Column 1, record dialogue and description that show Grover's panic, Percy's questions, and details about the storm. In Column 2, write what each detail reveals, or hints, about the truth regarding monsters and satyrs. Mark each detail with the page number."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Authors rarely tell everything at once. Riordan lets the truth come out in pieces, through what Grover says, what Percy asks, and what adults avoid saying. When we cite evidence, we point to the exact words and say what they show, whether the text says it directly or we have to infer it."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does Grover's behavior in this section show that he is afraid and that he knows more than he is saying? Cite a detail."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"On p. 45 Grover's bleating and nervous behavior show he is panicking. He seems to know that the danger is real, but he does not explain everything to Percy yet. That makes it feel like he is hiding the truth because he is afraid of how Percy will react."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What do Percy's questions tell us about what he wants?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy's questions show that he wants a straight answer. He asks what is going on because he does not feel safe, and he can tell the adults and Grover are leaving things out. His questions show he values the truth."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How do the storm details add to the way the truth is revealed?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The storm makes the danger seem bigger and out of control. When the weather is lashing the car, the characters have no time to explain, so the truth only comes out in small, rushed pieces."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Circulate and check that students quote or closely paraphrase and include page numbers. If a student cites a detail from a different chapter, steer them back to pp. 44–50. Page-level details may vary by edition, so accept any accurate detail from the assigned pages."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in reading closely and citing dialogue and description as evidence.","sayAsk":"Say: Point to the words that show Grover is scared. Frames: On page ___, the text says ___. This shows that ___. Percy asks ___ because he wants ___. Ask: What is the author telling you, and what is the author only hinting at? Let students first tell a partner in their home language, then in English.","watchFor":"If students retell the plot without citing, then ask: 'Which words on the page show that?' If students copy a long quote, then have them choose the most important four to six words. Success: student cites at least two details with page numbers and explains each with 'This shows...'"},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: choosing relevant evidence","tryThis":"Give a highlighted passage and ask: 'Who is speaking? What does this person feel? What is he or she not saying?' Then have the student record the detail and explanation using the frame 'This shows ___.'"},{"situation":"Ready for extension: inference","tryThis":"Ask students to find a detail where the truth is only hinted at and write an inference about what a character knows or fears, explaining why the text supports it."}]}]},{"id":"lia-word-choice-tension","title":"How Word Choice Builds Tension","minutes":12,"standards":["RL.6.1","L.6.4","L.6.6"],"routine":"Close Read and Word Choice Analysis","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 4","pages":"pp. 44–50"},{"type":"directions","text":"Choose three powerful words or phrases from pp. 44–50, such as *lashed*, *swerved*, *numb*, *wedged*, *slumped*, *spattered*, or *bulging*. For each one, write the sentence it appears in, a plainer word that could replace it, and what the author's word adds. Then write one sentence about how these word choices build tension or speed up the action."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"A word's meaning is its dictionary definition, but its connotation is the feeling it carries. *Lashed* and *hit* both mean struck, but *lashed* feels violent and angry. That feeling is how an author builds tension."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Replace *swerved* with *turned*. How does the scene change?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Turned sounds calm and slow. Swerved sounds sudden and dangerous, like the car almost crashed. The word swerved makes the action faster and the moment more tense."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Choose a word from p. 48 or p. 50. What does it make you picture, and what does it suggest about how the characters feel?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Slumped makes me picture someone who has no energy left and is giving up. It shows how hopeless and shocked the character feels, which makes the scene sadder and more serious."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.4","L.6.4"],"stem":"In Chapter 4, the author writes that the storm *lashed* the car. How does this word choice affect the scene?","choices":[{"text":"It makes the storm sound violent and harsh, which adds tension and danger.","correct":true,"rationale":"Correct. *Lashed* suggests a whip, so it gives the storm force and anger and raises tension."},{"text":"It shows that the storm is almost over and everyone can relax.","correct":false,"rationale":"This misreads the tone. *Lashed* is a forceful word and does not suggest the danger is ending."},{"text":"It tells readers that the car is tied to something.","correct":false,"rationale":"This confuses *lashed* with a meaning of tying down. In the context of the storm, it means hitting hard."},{"text":"It only tells readers it is raining, so the word choice does not matter.","correct":false,"rationale":"This ignores connotation. A plain word like *rained* would not carry the same violent feeling."}]},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Accept different word choices as long as students explain the effect with evidence. Push students beyond 'it sounds scary' by asking, 'What in the word makes it feel that way?'"},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in evaluating the author's language choices and expanding noun phrases to explain effect.","sayAsk":"Say: The author chose this word on purpose. Frames: Instead of ___, the author uses ___, which makes the scene feel ___. The word ___ suggests ___. The ___ storm that ___ the car creates ___. Ask: Which word is stronger, and why? Offer a word bank of feeling words: harsh, sudden, helpless, desperate, frightening.","watchFor":"If students say only 'it is a good word', then prompt: 'What picture or feeling does it give you?' If students confuse dictionary meaning with connotation, then compare two synonyms side by side. Success: student names a word, explains its connotation, and connects it to tension or action."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: explaining the effect of a word","tryThis":"Give a synonym pair, such as *hit/lashed* or *turned/swerved*, and ask which sounds more dangerous. Then supply the frame 'This word makes the scene feel ___ because ___.'"},{"situation":"Ready for extension: connotation and tone","tryThis":"Ask students to rewrite a sentence from the scene with calmer words and then explain how the tone and tension change."}]}]},{"id":"lia-explain-values-fears","title":"What Do Percy's Questions Suggest?","minutes":8,"standards":["RL.6.1","L.6.6"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Write a short paragraph of three to four sentences that answers the question: What do Percy's questions and reactions suggest about how people in this modern myth value safety and truth, and what they fear learning? Use at least two pieces of evidence from pp. 44–50 and at least one Chapter 4 vocabulary word."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Start with a claim, then cite dialogue or description, then explain it. Frames like 'The text shows...' and 'This suggests...' will help you."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Who in this part of the story seems to value safety most? Who values truth? How are they different?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy's mom and Grover seem to value safety most because they rush and hide parts of the story to keep Percy protected. Percy values truth because he keeps asking questions. They seem afraid that the truth will frighten or endanger him."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Model paragraph: Percy's questions suggest that he values truth, while the people around him value safety. When Percy asks what is happening, Grover bleats in panic and does not explain everything, which suggests he fears how Percy will react. The storm that lashed the car shows the danger is real, so the characters rush instead of talking. This suggests people in this modern myth fear that learning the truth about monsters will change Percy's life forever."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Collect these paragraphs as a formative check on RL.6.1. Look for a clear claim, accurate page-based evidence, and an explanation. Lesson 11 builds on this."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in writing a short explanation with evidence and precise noun phrases.","sayAsk":"Say: Rehearse your idea out loud before you write. Frames: Percy's questions suggest that ___. On page ___, the text says ___. This suggests that people fear ___ because ___. Ask: What do the characters protect, and what are they afraid will happen if Percy knows? Allow students to plan in their home language first and then write in English.","watchFor":"If students write opinions only ('I think Percy is brave'), then prompt: 'What does the text show?' If students list evidence without explanation, then prompt: 'Add a sentence that starts with This suggests...' Success: student states a claim, cites at least two details, and explains them."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: writing a claim supported by evidence","tryThis":"Provide a three-sentence frame: 'Percy's questions suggest ___. On page ___, the text shows ___. This suggests the characters fear ___.' Let the student say it to a partner before writing."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: values and fears","tryThis":"Ask students to explain how safety and truth sometimes conflict in the scene and to cite two details that show the conflict."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on how evidence and word choice help them understand how the truth is slowly revealed.","activities":[{"id":"lookback-reflection","title":"Exit Ticket: Word Choice and Tension","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.1","L.6.6"],"routine":"Reflection","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"In the Performance Task, you will analyze how word choice builds tension in a scene. Today you practiced finding powerful words and explaining their effect."},{"type":"directions","text":"Complete the sentences: One word from Chapter 4 that builds tension is ___. It makes the scene feel ___ because ___. Percy's questions suggest that he values ___, while other characters fear ___."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"One word from Chapter 4 that builds tension is swerved. It makes the scene feel sudden and dangerous because it shows the car turning fast to avoid something. Percy's questions suggest that he values the truth, while other characters fear scaring him with what the truth means."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework","purpose":"Students continue reading and begin comparing the novel with another myth tradition.","activities":[{"id":"homework-reading","title":"Read and Annotate","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.10"],"routine":"Independent Reading and Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"1) Read and annotate The Lightning Thief, Chapter 4 (pp. 51–56). Mark one detail about what the people in the story value and one thing they fear."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Homework is optional and counts 0 minutes. The annotations prepare students for Lesson 11 (writing about pp. 51–56) and for later cross-text comparison."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students reread Chapter 4 (pp. 44–50) of The Lightning Thief to cite dialogue and description showing how the truth about monsters and satyrs is slowly revealed.
